warmup.q: A coroutine on Dispatchers.Default runs for (lentil in sack) if (isStone(lentil)) stones++ over two million lentils, with no suspend calls inside the loop. Another coroutine calls job.cancel() halfway through. What happens?
options: The loop stops at once, because cancel() stops the coroutine's thread
The loop stops at the next lentil, because the compiler adds a check to every loop
The loop runs to the end, and only then does the job finish as cancelled
cancel() throws IllegalStateException, because the coroutine is busy
warmup.why: Cancellation is cooperative. cancel() only marks the job as cancelling. The coroutine notices at its next suspension point or explicit check, and this loop has neither, so it sorts all two million lentils first, like the helper who never looks up. Java's Future.cancel(true) has the same limit: it sets a flag that somebody has to read.

opening:
Halfway through the afternoon, the phone rings. The guests can't come: dinner is off. The cook turns the oven down, puts a lid on the soup and takes the sauce off the heat. She hears the news between two steps of a recipe, when she glances at her phone.

Her helper in the corner is picking small stones out of a big sack of lentils. He never looks up between lentils, so he hears nothing, and he sorts the whole sack.

Coroutines are called off the same way. It's natural to think cancel() stops the code, but it only asks, and the code has to look up. Structured concurrency sent a cancel down the tree, and Dispatchers and the coroutine context ended with a question: what does a coroutine do when it's cancelled in the middle of a long loop, or inside a blocking call?

In this lesson, we'll watch a cancel reach a coroutine between steps and miss a busy loop, stop a catch from eating it, return a borrowed pan after it, and put a timer on the whole thing. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with a dinner called off halfway, a cook who heard the news between steps, and a helper who sorted the whole sack. Coroutines hear a cancel only at suspension points and checks, carry it as CancellationException, and need NonCancellable to clean up after it. A timeout is the same cancel with a timer.

Now search your own code for runCatching and catch (e: Exception) around suspend calls. Each one that doesn't rethrow CancellationException turns the next cancel into a list of fake failures.

Next, we'll burn a dish instead of calling it off. When a coroutine fails, who hears about it, and how do you stop one burnt tray from spoiling the rest?

sections.h: A cancel is a request, heard only at suspension points and checks
sections.html:
Start with what cancel() really does. A coroutine is a piece of work that can pause and resume without holding its thread, the worker that runs the code. Every coroutine has a job, the handle to its life that you can wait for or cancel; Structured concurrency drew the tree of them. job.cancel() marks that job as cancelling, and that's all it does. It doesn't stop a thread, and it doesn't reach into the middle of your code.

The coroutine finds out at its next suspension point, a call to a suspend function where it may pause, such as delay, await, join or withContext. Those library calls look at the job first. When they find it cancelled, they throw CancellationException, the exception that carries a cancel through the code. It unwinds the stack, every finally block runs on the way out, and the job ends as cancelled. A coroutine that is already paused hears it at once: one waiting in delay(10_000) is woken with the exception straight away.

In the kitchen, a suspension point is the moment between two steps, when the cook glances at her phone. That's when the news reaches her.

Code that never reaches such a point never hears. Here's the helper with the lentils, a loop that is pure CPU work, which means calculation with no waiting in it:

Java
// Java equivalent: a loop that never reads the interrupt flag
int countStones(long[] lentils, LongPredicate isStone) {
    int stones = 0;
    for (long lentil : lentils) if (isStone.test(lentil)) stones++;
    return stones;
}
Kotlin
// Naive: never looks up from the sack
suspend fun countStones(lentils: LongArray, isStone: (Long) -> Boolean): Int {
    var stones = 0
    for (lentil in lentils) if (isStone(lentil)) stones++
    return stones
}

Nothing in the loop is a suspension point, so a cancel waits until the loop ends. This is cooperative cancellation: cancelling asks, and the code stops when it next checks. Java works the same way. Future.cancel(true) sets the thread's interrupt flag, a per-thread true-or-false value that asks it to stop (A thread's life, in the first track). A loop that never reads the flag keeps going.

CancelABusyLoop, in the Try it below, runs four loops over 60 million lentils on Dispatchers.Default, the pool for CPU work. It has one thread per core, the part of the processor that runs one thread at a time. Each loop is cancelled 100 ms after it starts. Predict how long each takes to stop. On this busy machine it printed:

no check                     stopped  2851 ms after cancel()
while (isActive)             stopped     4 ms after cancel()
ensureActive() every 1,000   stopped    10 ms after cancel()
yield() every 1,000          stopped     1 ms after cancel()

The loop with no check didn't stop when it was asked. It stopped when the sack was empty, almost three seconds later. (An idle machine sorts the whole sack in about 1.5 s.) The other three looked up now and then, and stopped within a few milliseconds.

Those three are the tools a CPU loop has. ensureActive() throws CancellationException if the job is cancelled. isActive returns a boolean, for a loop that wants to stop quietly: while (isActive) { ... }. yield() checks too, and also lets other coroutines waiting for the same thread run first. That matters when a long loop shares a small dispatcher, the part of the library that hands coroutines to threads. A check only reads the job's state, so it costs almost nothing, but once every thousand lentils is plenty:

Java
// Java equivalent: read the interrupt flag yourself
int countStones(long[] lentils, LongPredicate isStone) {
    int stones = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < lentils.length; i++) {
        if (i % 1_000 == 0 && Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted()) throw new CancellationException();
        if (isStone.test(lentils[i])) stones++;
    }
    return stones;
}
Kotlin
// Fixed: looks up every 1,000 lentils
suspend fun countStones(lentils: LongArray, isStone: (Long) -> Boolean): Int {
    val context = currentCoroutineContext()
    var stones = 0
    for ((i, lentil) in lentils.withIndex()) {
        if (i % 1_000 == 0) context.ensureActive()   // throws CancellationException once cancelled
        if (isStone(lentil)) stones++
    }
    return stones
}

Watch which job you are checking. Inside launch { }, isActive and ensureActive() belong to the coroutine you launched. A plain suspend function like countStones has no scope to call them on, so it reads its own context with currentCoroutineContext(). A bare isActive in a lambda nested inside another scope can quietly read the outer scope's job.

A cancel only asks. Code that never suspends or checks never hears it.

So a loop can be taught to look up. The next trap is a loop that looks up, hears the news, and throws it away.

try.title: Cancel four sorting loops
steps: Read CancelABusyLoop.kt. Each loop would sort its sack in about 1.5 s on an idle machine; the demo cancels it after 100 ms. Predict how long each one takes to stop.
Run it.
In the ensureActive() loop, change 1_000 to 10_000_000 and run it again. Predict first.
Run the Java twin, which uses Future.cancel(true) and the interrupt flag.

code.title: CancelABusyLoop.kt
code.html: package workbench.coroutines.l05 import kotlinx.coroutines.CoroutineScope import kotlinx.coroutines.Dispatchers import kotlinx.coroutines.cancelAndJoin import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.ensureActive import kotlinx.coroutines.isActive import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking import kotlinx.coroutines.yield /** Pure CPU work: looking at one lentil (a little arithmetic stands in for it). 60 million take about 1.5 s. */ private fun inspect(i: Long): Long { var x = i repeat(20) { x = x xor (x ushr 33) x *= -0xae502812aa7333L x = x xor (x ushr 29) } return x } private const val LENTILS = 60_000_000L @Volatile private var sink = 0L // keeps the JIT from deleting loops whose result nobody reads fun main() = runBlocking { // each loop gets the launched coroutine as its receiver, so isActive and ensureActive() look at // that coroutine's job (in a plain lambda they would quietly pick up runBlocking's scope instead) val loops: Map<String, suspend CoroutineScope.() -> Long> = mapOf( "no check" to { var sum = 0L for (i in 0 until LENTILS) sum += inspect(i) sum }, "while (isActive)" to { var sum = 0L var i = 0L while (isActive && i < LENTILS) { sum += inspect(i); i++ } sum }, "ensureActive() every 1,000" to { var sum = 0L for (i in 0 until LENTILS) { if (i % 1_000 == 0L) ensureActive() sum += inspect(i) } sum }, "yield() every 1,000" to { var sum = 0L for (i in 0 until LENTILS) { if (i % 1_000 == 0L) yield() sum += inspect(i) } sum }, ) for ((label, loop) in loops) { val job = launch(Dispatchers.Default) { sink = loop() } delay(100) // let it get going val asked = System.nanoTime() job.cancelAndJoin() println("%-28s stopped %5d ms after cancel()".format(label, (System.nanoTime() - asked) / 1_000_000)) } }

alt.title: CancelABusyLoopJava.java
alt.html: // Java equivalent of CancelABusyLoop.kt: Future.cancel(true) only sets the interrupt flag. // A CPU loop stops only if it looks at the flag. package workbench.coroutines.l05; import java.util.LinkedHashMap; import java.util.Map; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.Future; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; public class CancelABusyLoopJava { static final long LENTILS = 60_000_000L; static volatile long sink; // keeps the JIT from deleting loops whose result nobody reads /** Pure CPU work: looking at one lentil (a little arithmetic stands in for it). 60 million take about 1.5 s. */ static long inspect(long i) { long x = i; for (int k = 0; k < 20; k++) { x ^= x >>> 33; x *= -0xae502812aa7333L; x ^= x >>> 29; } return x; } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { Map<String, Runnable> loops = new LinkedHashMap<>(); loops.put("no check", () -> { long sum = 0; for (long i = 0; i < LENTILS; i++) sum += inspect(i); sink = sum; }); loops.put("isInterrupted() every 1,000", () -> { long sum = 0; for (long i = 0; i < LENTILS; i++) { if (i % 1_000 == 0 && Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted()) break; sum += inspect(i); } sink = sum; }); ExecutorService pool = Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor(); // one thread, so the no-op below waits for it for (var e : loops.entrySet()) { Future<?> f = pool.submit(e.getValue()); Thread.sleep(100); // let it get going long asked = System.nanoTime(); f.cancel(true); // sets the interrupt flag; the future reports "cancelled" at once // wait for the thread itself to come back: the no-op runs only once the loop has stopped pool.submit(() -> { }).get(); System.out.printf("%-28s stopped %5d ms after cancel(true)%n", e.getKey(), (System.nanoTime() - asked) / 1_000_000); } pool.shutdown(); pool.awaitTermination(10, TimeUnit.SECONDS); } }

try.expect: The loop with no check stops only when its sack is empty: about 1,400 ms after cancel() on an idle machine, and 2,851 ms here on a busy one. The other three stop within a few milliseconds (4, 10 and 1 ms here). With a check only every 10 million lentils, that loop stops late, at its next check, a few hundred milliseconds on. The Java twin shows the same split (1,425 and 0 ms here): cancel(true) reports success at once, but the loop that never reads the flag keeps its thread busy until it ends.

video.title: A cancel only asks: the cook hears it between steps while a loop with no check sorts the whole sack (2,851 ms), suspending cleanup needs NonCancellable to give the jam pan back, and a timeout is a cancel with a timer that a blocking call hears only through runInterruptible

sections.h: Never swallow the CancellationException that carries the cancel
sections.html:
Cancellation travels as an exception, and that is both its strength and its weak spot. The strength: CancellationException unwinds the stack, runs every finally, and closes every use block (Kotlin's way to close a resource) on the way out. The weak spot: a catch that catches it stops it right there.

Picture the evening before the big dinner. The cook phones each supplier in turn to confirm tomorrow's delivery. One busy line shouldn't stop the round, so every call is wrapped in runCatching, the standard function that runs a block and catches whatever it throws:

Java
// Java equivalent: catching InterruptedException and carrying on
for (String order : orders) {
    try { confirm(order); }
    catch (InterruptedException e) { System.out.println("call for " + order + " failed"); failed.add(order); }
}
Kotlin
// Naive: runCatching also catches the cancel
for (order in orders) {
    runCatching { confirm(order) }
        .onFailure { e -> println("call for $order failed, skipping: $e"); failed += order }
}

runCatching catches every Throwable. So do catch (e: Exception) and catch (e: Throwable), because on the JVM CancellationException is java.util.concurrent.CancellationException, a subclass of IllegalStateException.

Now the dinner is called off during the third call. Predict what the log shows. SwallowedCancellation, in the Try it below, phones the butcher every 100 ms, 20 times, and is cancelled at 250 ms:

runCatching, swallowing:
  calls before cancel: 3, after cancel: 17, cancelAndJoin took 8 ms

Seventeen more calls in 8 milliseconds, which is quick work even for a butcher. The coroutine was still cancelled, so every delay threw at once, runCatching caught it, and the loop went round again. Each "failed call" in the log was the cancel in disguise. A while (true) loop written this way is worse: it spins at full speed, forever.

That's the part that surprises people. Catching the exception doesn't undo the cancel. The job stays cancelled, so the code after the catch runs in a coroutine whose next suspension point throws again.

The Java twin fails differently, and the difference teaches something. Catching InterruptedException clears the thread's interrupt flag, so the next sleep sleeps normally. The swallowing Java loop made the same 17 calls at the usual pace, and shutdown took 1,719 ms. A swallowed interrupt is lost. A swallowed cancellation is still there, and every later suspension point throws it again.

The fix is to let it through. With runCatching, rethrow it first: .onFailure { if (it is CancellationException) throw it; ... }. With try, put catch (e: CancellationException) { throw e } before the general clause. Better still, catch only the exceptions you expect, such as IOException, and let everything else go up. With the rethrow in place, the same run printed after cancel: 0.

A cancel is an exception on its way out. Never catch it without rethrowing it.

So the cancel must be free to unwind the stack, finally blocks and all. But what can a finally block still do inside a coroutine that has been cancelled?

try.title: Swallow a cancel and count the damage
steps: Read SwallowedCancellation.kt. The round of calls is cancelled at 250 ms, after 3 calls. Predict how many calls happen after the cancel, and how long cancelAndJoin takes.
Run it.
Run it with -Pargs=fixed, which rethrows CancellationException.
Run the Java twin both ways and compare how long shutdown takes.

code.title: SwallowedCancellation.kt
code.html: package workbench.coroutines.l05 import kotlinx.coroutines.cancelAndJoin import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking import kotlin.coroutines.cancellation.CancellationException /** Phones the butcher 20 times, 100 ms apart, to ask if the order is ready. A failed call is logged and tried again. */ suspend fun phoneButcher(rethrowCancellation: Boolean, onCall: () -> Unit) { repeat(20) { runCatching { onCall() // the phone call to the butcher would go here delay(100) }.onFailure { e -> if (rethrowCancellation && e is CancellationException) throw e // swallowed: logged as a "failed call", and the loop goes round again } } } fun main(args: Array<String>) = runBlocking { val fixed = args.firstOrNull() == "fixed" var calls = 0 var cancelledAt = -1 val caller = launch { phoneButcher(rethrowCancellation = fixed) { calls++ } } delay(250) cancelledAt = calls val asked = System.nanoTime() caller.cancelAndJoin() val ms = (System.nanoTime() - asked) / 1_000_000 println(if (fixed) "runCatching + rethrow:" else "runCatching, swallowing:") println(" calls before cancel: $cancelledAt, after cancel: ${calls - cancelledAt}, cancelAndJoin took $ms ms") }

alt.title: SwallowedCancellationJava.java
alt.html: // Java equivalent of SwallowedCancellation.kt: catching InterruptedException and carrying on // swallows the cancel request, just as runCatching swallows CancellationException. package workbench.coroutines.l05; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; public class SwallowedCancellationJava { /** Phones the butcher 20 times, 100 ms apart. A failed call is logged and tried again. */ static void phoneButcher(boolean restoreInterrupt, AtomicInteger calls) { for (int i = 0; i < 20; i++) { try { calls.incrementAndGet(); // the phone call to the butcher would go here Thread.sleep(100); } catch (InterruptedException e) { if (restoreInterrupt) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); return; // stop: somebody asked us to } // swallowed: the flag is now clear, so the next sleep() sleeps normally } } } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { boolean fixed = args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("fixed"); AtomicInteger calls = new AtomicInteger(); ExecutorService pool = Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor(); pool.submit(() -> phoneButcher(fixed, calls)); Thread.sleep(250); int cancelledAt = calls.get(); long asked = System.nanoTime(); pool.shutdownNow(); // interrupts the caller pool.awaitTermination(10, TimeUnit.SECONDS); long ms = (System.nanoTime() - asked) / 1_000_000; System.out.println(fixed ? "catch + restore the flag:" : "catch, swallowing:"); System.out.printf(" calls before cancel: %d, after cancel: %d, shutdown took %d ms%n", cancelledAt, calls.get() - cancelledAt, ms); } }

try.expect: Swallowing: 3 calls before the cancel and 17 after, and cancelAndJoin returns within a few milliseconds (8 ms here), because every remaining delay threw at once. Fixed: 0 calls after the cancel. The swallowing Java twin also makes 17 more calls, but over about 1.7 s (1,719 ms here): catching the interrupt cleared the flag, so the later sleeps were normal sleeps. Restoring the flag and returning stops it at once (1 ms here).

aside.title: Is cancelling a coroutine the same as interrupting its thread?
aside.html: No, though the two ideas are cousins. A cancel marks the coroutine's job and leaves the thread alone, so Thread.sleep and other blocking JDK calls don't notice it. An interrupt marks a thread, and suspension points such as delay ignore it. The job's state also lasts: it reaches every child in the tree, and no catch can clear it, while catching InterruptedException clears the flag. The last section of this lesson shows runInterruptible, which turns a cancel into an interrupt for the blocking code that needs one.

sections.h: Cleanup after a cancel: give the pan back inside NonCancellable
sections.html:
Picture the cook making jam in a big pan borrowed from the community kitchen down the road. The jam takes a while to set, and the pan must go back afterwards, whatever happens. Giving it back means phoning the lending desk, so giveBack is a suspend function. The natural shape is try and finally:

Java
// Java equivalent: once the flag is set again, blocking cleanup fails at once
String ticket = desk.lend("jam-pan");
try {
    waitForTheJamToSet();
} catch (InterruptedException e) {
    Thread.currentThread().interrupt();   // keep the cancel request, as you should
} finally {
    desk.giveBack(ticket);                // blocks, sees the flag, throws InterruptedException
}
Kotlin
// Naive: after a cancel, the pan stays in our kitchen
val ticket = desk.lend("jam-pan")
try {
    waitForTheJamToSet()        // cancelled here
} finally {
    desk.giveBack(ticket)       // suspends, so it throws at once
}

The finally block runs, as promised. But it runs inside a coroutine that is still cancelled, and there every suspension point throws CancellationException at once. giveBack never gets past its first one. CleanupAfterCancel, in the Try it below, calls the jam off at 100 ms:

  borrowed the jam pan on ticket-7
cancel, plain suspend call in finally:
  giving back failed at once: JobCancellationException
  jam job finished, cancelled = true

JobCancellationException is the library's own subclass of CancellationException. The jam is off, and the pan is still in our kitchen. The community kitchen would like a word.

The fix is one wrapper: finally { withContext(NonCancellable) { desk.giveBack(ticket) } }. NonCancellable is a job that is always active. Inside that block, suspension points don't throw, so the call runs to the end. The coroutine itself stays cancelled: when the block finishes, the CancellationException carries on up the stack as before. Run with -Pargs=fixed, the demo printed gave back the pan on ticket-7 about 50 ms after the cancel, and the job still finished as cancelled.

Use it in exactly this shape: withContext(NonCancellable), inside a finally, around the cleanup call and nothing else. The docs warn against launch(NonCancellable) or async(NonCancellable). A job passed to a builder replaces the parent, so the new coroutine leaves the tree: nothing waits for it, and nothing can cancel it. Lesson 6 of this track shows the same trap with another job. Keep the cleanup short, too. Nothing will cancel it for you, so a slow call inside it needs its own timeout, which the next section builds.

Cleanup that doesn't suspend needs nothing special. Closing a file is an ordinary call, not a suspending one, and it runs fine in a cancelled coroutine.

A cancelled coroutine can't suspend. Wrap suspending cleanup in withContext(NonCancellable).

So far the guests have phoned to call things off. Often nobody phones. You decide in advance how long you're willing to wait.

try.title: Keep the pan, then give it back
steps: Read CleanupAfterCancel.kt. The jam is called off while it sets. Predict whether gave back the pan prints.
Run it.
Run it with -Pargs=fixed, which wraps giveBack in withContext(NonCancellable).
Run the Java twin both ways.

code.title: CleanupAfterCancel.kt
code.html: package workbench.coroutines.l05 import kotlinx.coroutines.NonCancellable import kotlinx.coroutines.cancelAndJoin import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking import kotlinx.coroutines.withContext import kotlin.coroutines.cancellation.CancellationException private suspend fun giveBack(ticket: String) { delay(50) // the phone call to the lending desk println(" gave back the pan on $ticket") } fun main(args: Array<String>) = runBlocking { val fixed = args.firstOrNull() == "fixed" val jam = launch { val ticket = "ticket-7" println(" borrowed the jam pan on $ticket") try { delay(10_000) // waiting for the jam to set } finally { try { if (fixed) withContext(NonCancellable) { giveBack(ticket) } else giveBack(ticket) } catch (e: CancellationException) { println(" giving back failed at once: ${e::class.simpleName}") throw e } } } delay(100) println(if (fixed) "cancel, giveBack inside withContext(NonCancellable):" else "cancel, plain suspend call in finally:") jam.cancelAndJoin() println(" jam job finished, cancelled = ${jam.isCancelled}") }

alt.title: CleanupAfterCancelJava.java
alt.html: // Java equivalent of CleanupAfterCancel.kt: a thread that was interrupted can't make a blocking // cleanup call while its interrupt flag is set. Clear the flag for the cleanup, then restore it. package workbench.coroutines.l05; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; public class CleanupAfterCancelJava { static void giveBack(String ticket) throws InterruptedException { Thread.sleep(50); // the phone call to the lending desk System.out.println(" gave back the pan on " + ticket); } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { boolean fixed = args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("fixed"); ExecutorService pool = Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor(); pool.submit(() -> { String ticket = "ticket-7"; System.out.println(" borrowed the jam pan on " + ticket); try { Thread.sleep(10_000); // waiting for the jam to set } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); // keep the cancel request, as you should } finally { boolean wasInterrupted = fixed && Thread.interrupted(); // fixed: clear the flag for cleanup try { giveBack(ticket); } catch (InterruptedException e) { System.out.println(" giving back failed at once: InterruptedException"); Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } if (wasInterrupted) Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); // and put it back afterwards } }); Thread.sleep(100); System.out.println(fixed ? "interrupt, flag cleared around giveBack:" : "interrupt, plain blocking call in finally:"); pool.shutdownNow(); pool.awaitTermination(10, TimeUnit.SECONDS); System.out.println(" task finished"); } }

try.expect: Without the wrapper, giving back failed at once: JobCancellationException prints, and the pan is never returned. With -Pargs=fixed, gave back the pan on ticket-7 prints about 50 ms after the cancel, and the job still finishes as cancelled. The Java twin fails the same way with InterruptedException, and its fix is to clear the flag around the cleanup and restore it afterwards.

sections.h: A timeout is a cancel with a timer, and blocking calls don't hear it
sections.html:
Before a big dinner, the cook also sets a kitchen timer on the bread order: if the bakery hasn't answered in a few minutes, she bakes her own. withTimeout(d) { ... } is that timer. It runs the block, and when d runs out, it cancels the block. The cancel is the ordinary kind from the first section: the block stops at its next suspension point, and withTimeout throws TimeoutCancellationException. withTimeoutOrNull(d) { ... } does the same, but returns null instead of throwing:

Java
// Java equivalent: a fallback value when the future is late
String answer = bakery.askAsync("sourdough")
    .completeOnTimeout("no answer: bake our own", 300, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)
    .join();
Kotlin
val answer = withTimeoutOrNull(300.milliseconds) { bakery.ask("sourdough") }
    ?: "no answer: bake our own"

Prefer withTimeoutOrNull when a timeout is an outcome you expect, as it is here. TimeoutCancellationException is a subclass of CancellationException, and that has a surprising effect. Inside launch, a timeout looks like an ordinary cancel, so a child that times out inside coroutineScope lets the scope finish normally, and nobody hears about it. If a timeout should fail the caller, turn it into a real error: withTimeoutOrNull(d) { ... } ?: error("the bakery never answered").

A timer is still a cancel, and a cancel still only asks. So what happens when the block is stuck in a blocking call, one that holds its thread until it returns? The bakery from lesson 4 of this track still has an old order line, BakeryHotline, whose ask blocks the thread until somebody picks up. Let's wait 300 ms, and let the bakery take 1.5 s. TimeoutsAndBlocking, in the Try it below, tries four shapes, with Thread.sleep standing in for the call:

withTimeout { delay }                              threw TimeoutCancellationException   after   307 ms
withTimeoutOrNull { delay }                        returned null                        after   304 ms
withTimeout { withContext(IO) { sleep } }          threw TimeoutCancellationException   after  1519 ms
withTimeoutOrNull { runInterruptible { sleep } }   returned null                        after   301 ms

The two delay lines stopped on time. The third line is the trap. The timer fired at 300 ms, but a thread blocked in Thread.sleep isn't at a suspension point. The thread stayed on the old phone line, listening to it ring, long after the timer had given up. Only when the call ended at 1.5 s did withContext notice the cancel and throw. The Dispatchers.IO thread, from the pool for blocking calls, was stuck the whole time. When the blocking call is the whole block, with no suspension at all, the timeout is ignored entirely, and the late answer comes back as if nothing had happened.

The fourth line is the fix. runInterruptible(dispatcher) { ... } runs blocking code on that dispatcher, and when the coroutine is cancelled, it interrupts the thread. It turns the resulting InterruptedException back into a CancellationException, so the caller sees an ordinary cancel:

Java
// Java equivalent: give up after the timeout and interrupt the worker
Future<String> f = io.submit(() -> hotline.ask("sourdough"));
try { return f.get(300, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS); }
catch (TimeoutException e) { f.cancel(true); return null; }   // interrupts the blocked thread
Kotlin
withTimeoutOrNull(300.milliseconds) {
    runInterruptible(Dispatchers.IO) { hotline.ask("sourdough") }   // interrupted on cancel
}

Here the kitchen picture breaks. A cook can put the phone down whenever she likes. runInterruptible can only interrupt, and that helps only if the blocking call listens for interrupts. Thread.sleep and BlockingQueue.take do. A read from an old-style java.net.Socket network connection doesn't, and database drivers vary, so give such a client its own timeout as well.

A timeout is a cancel with a timer. A blocking call hears it only through runInterruptible.

That covers the places a cancel can get lost. A cancel, though, is the polite way for a coroutine to end. The next lesson takes the rude one: a coroutine that fails.

try.title: Time out the bakery four ways
steps: Read TimeoutsAndBlocking.kt. The bakery takes 1.5 s to answer and every call waits 300 ms. Predict the outcome and the time for each line.
Run it.
Delete the withContext(Dispatchers.IO) wrapper in the third case, leaving withTimeout(300) { Thread.sleep(1_500); "bread ready" }. Predict, then run.
Run the Java twin and compare orTimeout with get plus cancel(true).

code.title: TimeoutsAndBlocking.kt
code.html: package workbench.coroutines.l05 import kotlinx.coroutines.Dispatchers import kotlinx.coroutines.TimeoutCancellationException import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking import kotlinx.coroutines.runInterruptible import kotlinx.coroutines.withContext import kotlinx.coroutines.withTimeout import kotlinx.coroutines.withTimeoutOrNull /** Runs [block] and prints what came out and how long it took. */ private suspend fun timed(label: String, block: suspend () -> Any?) { val t0 = System.nanoTime() val outcome = try { "returned ${block()}" } catch (e: TimeoutCancellationException) { "threw TimeoutCancellationException" } println("%-50s %-36s after %5d ms".format(label, outcome, (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000)) } fun main() = runBlocking { // the bakery takes 1.5 s to answer; we wait 300 ms timed("withTimeout { delay }") { withTimeout(300) { delay(1_500); "bread ready" } } timed("withTimeoutOrNull { delay }") { withTimeoutOrNull(300) { delay(1_500); "bread ready" } } timed("withTimeout { withContext(IO) { sleep } }") { withTimeout(300) { withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { Thread.sleep(1_500); "bread ready" } } } timed("withTimeoutOrNull { runInterruptible { sleep } }") { withTimeoutOrNull(300) { runInterruptible(Dispatchers.IO) { Thread.sleep(1_500); "bread ready" } } } }

alt.title: TimeoutsAndBlockingJava.java
alt.html: // Java equivalent of TimeoutsAndBlocking.kt: a timeout on a CompletableFuture gives the caller // an answer on time, but nothing stops the blocking task. Future.cancel(true) interrupts it. package workbench.coroutines.l05; import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture; import java.util.concurrent.CompletionException; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.Future; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; import java.util.concurrent.TimeoutException; public class TimeoutsAndBlockingJava { static long t0; static String callBakery() { try { Thread.sleep(1_500); // the bakery takes 1.5 s to answer System.out.printf(" (the bakery call itself finished at %d ms)%n", ms()); return "bread ready"; } catch (InterruptedException e) { System.out.printf(" (the bakery call was interrupted at %d ms)%n", ms()); return "interrupted"; } } static long ms() { return (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000; } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { try (ExecutorService io = Executors.newCachedThreadPool()) { // 1. orTimeout: the caller gets a TimeoutException on time, the task runs on t0 = System.nanoTime(); try { CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(TimeoutsAndBlockingJava::callBakery, io).orTimeout(300, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS).join(); } catch (CompletionException e) { System.out.printf("orTimeout(300 ms) caller got %s after %d ms%n", e.getCause().getClass().getSimpleName(), ms()); } Thread.sleep(1_400); // wait, to see the abandoned task finish anyway // 2. Future.get with a timeout, then cancel(true): the blocked thread is interrupted t0 = System.nanoTime(); Future<String> f = io.submit(TimeoutsAndBlockingJava::callBakery); try { f.get(300, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS); } catch (TimeoutException e) { f.cancel(true); System.out.printf("get(300 ms) + cancel(true) caller gave up after %d ms%n", ms()); } Thread.sleep(100); } } }

try.expect: The two delay cases end at about 300 ms (307 and 304 ms here): one throws, one returns null. The withContext(IO) case throws too, but only after about 1,500 ms (1,519 ms here), when the sleep is over. runInterruptible returns null at about 300 ms. After your change, the bare sleep returns bread ready after 1,500 ms: the block never suspended, so the timeout was ignored. In the Java twin, orTimeout gives the caller its exception on time (320 ms here) while the abandoned call finishes at 1,519 ms anyway, and cancel(true) interrupts the call at about 300 ms.

compare.title: Stopping a CPU loop: Future.cancel(true) vs Job.cancel()

java.title: LentilSort.java
java.html: Future<Integer> f = pool.submit(() -> { int stones = 0; for (int i = 0; i < lentils.length; i++) { if (i % 1_000 == 0 && Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted()) { throw new CancellationException("sorting stopped at " + i); // 1. look at the flag } if (isStone(lentils[i])) stones++; } return stones; }); f.cancel(true); // 2. sets the worker's interrupt flag; the loop stops at its next check

kotlin.title: LentilSort.kt
kotlin.html: val job = scope.async(Dispatchers.Default) { var stones = 0 for ((i, lentil) in lentils.withIndex()) { if (i % 1_000 == 0) ensureActive() // 1. throws CancellationException once cancelled if (isStone(lentil)) stones++ } stones } job.cancel() // 2. marks the job cancelled; the loop stops at its next check

compare.note: Both models are cooperative, and both loops need the same explicit check, once every thousand lentils. The difference is what carries the request. Java's interrupt is a flag on one thread. It doesn't reach other threads the task started, and catching InterruptedException clears it, so a careless catch loses it for good. A coroutine's cancel is a state on its job. It reaches every child in the tree, it stays set whatever you catch, and every suspension point in the library checks it for you, so most coroutine code needs no explicit check at all. Only CPU loops like this one, and blocking calls (which need runInterruptible), have to be taught to look up.

worked.title: Make an oven watcher stop cleanly

steps.say: The community kitchen has shared ovens. This function books one, then checks every 5 seconds whether the bread is done. When the cook calls the evening off, the function seems to hang, and the oven stays booked, so nobody else can use it. Find the three problems before you read on.
steps.code: suspend fun waitForBread(loaf: String): Bread { val booking = ovens.book(loaf) try { while (true) { try { val bread = ovens.check(loaf) if (bread.isDone) return bread delay(5.seconds) } catch (e: Exception) { log.warn("oven check failed for $loaf", e) } } } finally { ovens.release(booking) // suspend: a phone call to the community kitchen } }

alt.html: // Java equivalent of the same bugs Bread waitForBread(String loaf) { Booking booking = ovens.book(loaf); try { while (true) { try { Bread bread = ovens.check(loaf); if (bread.isDone()) return bread; Thread.sleep(5_000); } catch (Exception e) { // also catches InterruptedException log.warn("oven check failed for {}", loaf, e); } } } finally { ovens.release(booking); // fails at once if the flag is set } }

steps.say: Problem 1: catch (e: Exception) swallows the CancellationException from delay, so a cancelled watcher spins. Catch only the oven's own error, and let the cancel through.
steps.code: while (true) { try { val bread = ovens.check(loaf) if (bread.isDone) return bread } catch (e: OvenException) { // 1. only what we expect from the call log.warn("oven check failed for $loaf", e) } delay(5.seconds) // outside the try: a cancel ends the loop }

alt.html: while (true) { try { Bread bread = ovens.check(loaf); if (bread.isDone()) return bread; } catch (OvenException e) { // 1. only what we expect from the call log.warn("oven check failed for {}", loaf, e); } Thread.sleep(5_000); // InterruptedException now propagates }

steps.say: Problem 2: the release suspends in a cancelled coroutine, so it throws before the phone even rings. Wrap it in NonCancellable, with its own short timeout, so a phone nobody answers can't hold up the evening.
steps.code: } finally { // 2. cleanup that suspends must run non-cancellable, and bounded withContext(NonCancellable) { withTimeoutOrNull(2.seconds) { ovens.release(booking) } } }

alt.html: } finally { // 2. clear the flag for the cleanup, then restore it boolean interrupted = Thread.interrupted(); try { ovens.release(booking); } finally { if (interrupted) Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } }

steps.say: Problem 3: nothing bounds the whole wait. Give the caller a deadline, and treat running out as an expected outcome rather than an exception.
steps.code: // 3. the caller decides how long the bread may take val bread: Bread? = withTimeoutOrNull(10.minutes) { waitForBread("rye") } if (bread == null) bakeFlatbread() // plan B

alt.html: // 3. the caller decides how long the bread may take Future<Bread> f = pool.submit(() -> waitForBread("rye")); try { serve(f.get(10, TimeUnit.MINUTES)); } catch (TimeoutException e) { f.cancel(true); bakeFlatbread(); }

steps.say: Self-check: the timeout in step 3 cancels waitForBread while it is suspended in delay. Trace what happens. (The delay throws TimeoutCancellationException, which passes the narrow catch. The finally releases the oven under NonCancellable, and withTimeoutOrNull turns the exception into null.)

lab.title: Fix four cancellation bugs in the kitchen
steps: Meet the code. Each file holds one small kitchen job, and each stub is the buggy code, with a KDoc that says what's wrong. countStones picks through a sack of lentils, confirmEach phones each supplier in turn, withBorrowed borrows a pan from the lending desk and must always give it back, and askBakery asks the bakery's old blocking phone line. Run the tests: four of eight fail, one per file.
SortLentils.kt: make countStones check for cancellation at least once every 1,000 lentils.
SupplierCalls.kt: keep runCatching, but make a CancellationException end the round instead of being logged as a failed call.
BorrowedPot.kt: make the giveBack call in finally run to the end even when the caller was cancelled.
BakeryHotline.kt: return null on timeout instead of throwing, and make the timeout interrupt the blocked ask call.
Run the tests until all eight pass, then run them once more.
hints: countStones is a plain suspend function with no scope, so call currentCoroutineContext().ensureActive(). Read the context once, before the loop.
Import CancellationException from kotlin.coroutines.cancellation (or kotlinx.coroutines). Both name the same class.
runInterruptible(Dispatchers.IO) { ... } replaces withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { ... } for blocking code that should be interrupted on cancel.
lab.done: All eight tests in CancellationTest pass, twice in a row.

drill.title: A cancellable job from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write suspend fun labelJars(jars: List<Jar>, loan: Loan) that runs on Dispatchers.Default, checks for cancellation every 500 jars, and calls label(jar), which can throw LabelException (log it and skip that jar). It must always return the borrowed label printer with the suspending loan.giveBack(), even after a cancel.

answer.html: suspend fun labelJars(jars: List<Jar>, loan: Loan) { try { withContext(Dispatchers.Default) { for ((i, jar) in jars.withIndex()) { if (i % 500 == 0) ensureActive() // cooperate with a cancel try { label(jar) } catch (e: LabelException) { // only what we expect log.warn("skipping ${jar.id}", e) } } } } finally { withContext(NonCancellable) { loan.giveBack() } // suspending cleanup } }

alt.title: Java equivalent
alt.html: // Java equivalent: read the interrupt flag, clear it around the cleanup void labelJars(List<Jar> jars, Loan loan) { try { for (int i = 0; i < jars.size(); i++) { if (i % 500 == 0 && Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted()) return; // cooperate with a cancel try { label(jars.get(i)); } catch (LabelException e) { // only what we expect log.warn("skipping {}", jars.get(i).id(), e); } } } finally { boolean interrupted = Thread.interrupted(); try { loan.giveBack(); } // blocking cleanup finally { if (interrupted) Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } } }

recap: Cancellation is cooperative. cancel() marks the job, and the coroutine stops at its next suspension point or explicit check. CPU loops need ensureActive(), isActive or yield().
Cancellation travels as CancellationException. runCatching, catch (e: Exception) and catch (e: Throwable) all catch it, so rethrow it or catch narrower types. Catching it never undoes the cancel.
In a cancelled coroutine every suspension point throws at once. Run suspending cleanup in finally inside withContext(NonCancellable), and never pass NonCancellable to launch or async.
withTimeout throws TimeoutCancellationException (a CancellationException), and withTimeoutOrNull returns null. Inside launch, a timeout doesn't fail the parent unless you turn it into an error.
The limit: a cancel only asks. Blocking code hears it only through runInterruptible, and only if the call responds to interrupts; for the rest, give the client its own timeout.

explain.prompt: A friend wrapped every call in the evening's supplier round in runCatching, "so one busy line never stops the round". When the dinner was called off, the log listed seventeen failed calls that had never failed. Explain what happened and how you'd change the code.
explain.answer: Calling the dinner off cancelled the coroutine running the round. A cancel reaches the code as a CancellationException thrown from the next suspension point, and runCatching catches every Throwable, so it caught that too and logged the call in progress as failed. Catching it didn't undo the cancel: the coroutine was still cancelled, so the next call threw at its first suspension point, got caught and logged the same way, and so on through all seventeen remaining calls. Then the function returned normally. I'd keep the per-call error handling, but rethrow CancellationException before logging anything, or catch only the exceptions a phone call is expected to throw. Then a cancel ends the round at the call in progress, and any cleanup that suspends goes in a finally inside withContext(NonCancellable).

deeper.html:
A CancellationException doesn't always mean "I was cancelled". If you await() a Deferred that someone else cancelled, await throws CancellationException in your coroutine, even though your coroutine is fine. The kotlinx.coroutines 1.11 KDoc calls this a legacy behavior that can't be changed compatibly: your coroutine then ends as "cancelled", so its parent isn't told and the work quietly stops. If you catch it, call currentCoroutineContext().ensureActive() in the catch. It throws only if your coroutine was cancelled, so after it you know the exception came from the thing you awaited, and you can turn it into a real error.

The library also gives a prompt cancellation guarantee. If a coroutine is cancelled while suspended, it resumes with CancellationException even when the value it was waiting for had already arrived. withContext checks for cancellation both on entry and when its block returns. So val pan = withContext(io) { desk.lendBlocking() } can lose a pan: the block borrowed it, the caller was cancelled in the meantime, and the result is thrown away. Borrow and give back inside the same block, or use the cleanup function of CancellableContinuation.resume when you write the bridge yourself (lesson 1 of this track).

Timeouts have one more subtle rule. The KDoc says cancellation on timeout "may happen at any time, even after the block finishes executing but before the caller gets resumed". So never write withTimeout { pan = desk.lend() } and expect pan to be either unset or yours. Borrow outside the timeout, or give it back in the block's own finally.

Flows, which lesson 7 of this track introduces, have the same cooperative rule at a smaller scale. A flow { } builder checks for cancellation at every emit, but list.asFlow() and (1..n).asFlow() don't, so add .cancellable() to a long one that must stop on time.

Finally, runBlocking bridges in the other direction. If the thread blocked in runBlocking is interrupted, the coroutine is cancelled, and runBlocking throws InterruptedException. That's how coroutine code called from a plain Java worker thread can still be stopped by an executor's shutdownNow().
